structure.title: Descriptive evidence from 100 years of land-use data

observations.statement: The empirical strategy is named as a staggered difference-in-differences design; the estimand is a cohort-time average treatment effect defined as a difference in outcome changes between treated and untreated plots of the same cohort, written out as an equation before the estimator is introduced.

The authors motivate the doubly-robust estimator by naming two threats: time-varying selection into treatment that biases two-way fixed effects under staggered adoption, and weather-driven variability in the outcome, addressed by cohort-specific propensity matching and outcome regression adjustment.
A footnote explains why a boundary regression discontinuity design was rejected: protected-area borders follow land-use breaks, so land cover and treatment change simultaneously at the boundary.

The identifying variation is described as changes in greenness over time in protected versus observably similar unprotected plots combined with staggered protection timing; parallel trends are argued via matched controls and inspected in event-time plots.
A dynamic siting model of a planner versus a delegated local policymaker is developed first and yields four numbered predictions that the empirical section later maps results onto one by one.

Two gridded panels are assembled: a fine grid for vegetation cover and a coarser grid for nightlights, covering the EU plus several non-member countries at biennial frequency over the sample window; each of six data types is named with its provider.
Country exclusions due to missing data and the handling of protected areas with missing foundation dates (hand-collected for the largest cases) are documented in footnotes.
Marine reserves are excluded; observations with negative NDVI are dropped as they correspond to snow, water and clouds; biennial summer aggregation is used to limit cloud-induced missingness.
observations.locator: Section 4, Policy rollout and Vegetation cover

observations.statement: To allow parallel-trend checks, cohorts treated within the first three biennial periods are excluded so the earliest cohort has pre-periods; event-study panels additionally require units in sample three periods before and after treatment, dropping the earliest and latest cohorts.

For computational and memory reasons, some estimations use a random sample of never-treated land as controls within each country and a stratified random sample of the EU for the causal forest; this is stated in table notes and footnotes.
A known shapefile artefact for one country (large designated areas missing from the CDDA database) is disclosed in a footnote rather than corrected.

Treatment is defined at the grid level: a cell is treated if any non-zero fraction of its area falls in a designated protected area, with the cohort given by the first protection year; never-treated cells are assigned an infinite cohort date.

The primary outcome is a rescaled continuous vegetation index built from Landsat imagery; the authors justify the choice against discrete land-use classes by citing classification error literature and validate it against discrete land-use categories and bird richness studies.
Nightlights are explicitly framed as a proxy for human presence rather than GDP, with the criticisms of the nightlights literature acknowledged.

Covariates for the propensity score and outcome adjustment are chosen from prior agronomic literature on yields: fixed land factors, time-varying weather, and baseline levels and pre-period trend of the outcome.
Protection strictness is coded as a binary index from IUCN categories, with the mapping stated in figure notes and an alternative grouping mentioned in a footnote.

The headline figure shows the preferred doubly-robust estimate alongside two two-way fixed effects variants (with and without matching) in a top panel and country-level estimates with bootstrapped intervals in a bottom panel; regression tables are relegated to the appendix.

The country-level bivariate regression table reports one covariate per column, R2, observations, the independent variable mean, states that standard errors are iid at the country level and that regressions are weighted by inverse standard errors of the first-stage estimates.
The two-way fixed effects benchmark is written as an equation with grid and time fixed effects in a footnote, with dynamic versions in the appendix.

Aggregation from country-cohort-time effects to country, EU-wide, event-time and cohort averages is written out with explicit weight formulas; the authors note that weights are observed rather than estimated because the data cover all land.

Standard errors come from the multiplier bootstrap; clustering is at the protected-area identifier because plots are assigned to treatment together, in addition to the default plot-level clustering of the estimator, citing Bertrand et al.
observations.quote: we cluster at the assignment level of the CDDA identifier

observations.statement: A footnote acknowledges that EU-level standard errors ignore covariance across country-level effects, defends this by independent member-state decisions, and cites computational cost as a further motivation.
The causal forest is motivated partly as a way to avoid multiple testing across many candidate heterogeneity dimensions, with a formal test for deviation from the average effect.
A descriptive balance table compares land characteristics by deforestation status in the main text; balance tables with and without cohort-specific matching are placed in the appendix.

Pre-treatment coefficients are shown in event-time figures; a footnote notes that some pre-period coefficients are statistically distinguishable from zero but small, citing sensitivity work on parallel trends.
A high-population subsample is reported to fail the parallel pre-trend check and is discussed as such rather than dropped silently.

Robustness checks are summarised in a single paragraph pointing to an appendix: first-differenced outcome for functional form, restriction to greener plots, not-yet-treated controls, a high-population subsample, and a spatial first difference model.
Standard two-way fixed effects results are reported for completeness in an appendix as a benchmark to the preferred estimator.
Consistency with discrete land-use data is checked via a matched transition-matrix comparison over a fixed window, with the matching variables listed in the text.
Absence of cohort trends is formalised with two country-level tests (linear trend in cohort effects and early versus late cohort difference) reported in an appendix table.

Conditional average treatment effects are estimated with an honest causal forest adapted to a difference-in-differences setting, and plotted across ventiles of key covariates; heterogeneity is tied to the model's siting predictions.
Average effects are re-estimated separately by protection strictness category and by country; country-level effects are then regressed on political-economy covariates one at a time.

Effects are benchmarked against the index gap between land-use classes, the within-country standard deviation of the outcome, and cross-country differences in nightlights; the null is characterised by the tightness of confidence intervals.

The discussion walks through each model prediction to identify which combination of political-economy features rationalises the results, then considers and argues against explanations outside the model.
Descriptive facts on siting and strictness patterns, and country-level correlations with enforcement proxies, are used as evidence about mechanisms.
The authors state repeatedly that the vegetation index cannot capture all biodiversity dimensions targeted by the policy and that species-count data allow only non-causal descriptive checks.
Unavailability of land-ownership data across countries is noted as a limitation in a footnote.
Spillovers are dismissed as a concern conditional on the null result, with reference to studies where spillovers arise under positive effects.
The authors argue the model mechanisms are likely more salient in low-income forest-rich countries and position the EU evidence as informative for the global protection target.

Descriptive evidence uses maps of outcome levels and changes inside and outside protected areas, heatmap-style bin plots of protection probability by baseline greenness and density, and a balance-style summary table.

Event-time and cohort effects are plotted with bootstrapped confidence bands and a lower panel showing the number of treated cells per bin; notes state trimming of event-time windows and point to appendix tables.

Stars appear only in the country-level correlation table with a single threshold explained in notes; other tables report estimates with standard errors in parentheses and describe the sample in notes.
Appendix tables and figures are numbered with an A prefix and referenced throughout the main text for regression results behind each figure.
The introduction enumerates three contributions, four descriptive facts, and six numbered findings, then closes with a literature positioning and a section roadmap.
Order is background, theoretical model with predictions, data, descriptive facts, methodology, results, conclusion; robustness is folded into the results section with details in appendices.
Main text relies on appendices for regression tables, estimation details, balance tables, robustness and species-count analyses (Appendices A-E).
A data availability statement gives a Zenodo DOI for data and code, notes that third-party data could not be redistributed, and says the package includes instructions for obtaining them.
The grf software package is named for the causal forest estimation.

Outcomes and treatment come from public remote-sensing and EU designated-area databases merged onto grids with climate, soil and topography layers from public European agencies; country covariates are from public statistical and NGO-monitoring sources.

gaps: No discussion of few-cluster issues; cluster counts are only implied by the number of CDDA areas.
No preregistration or ethics statement (not expected for remote-sensing data).
No summary statistics table for the estimation sample in the main text; Table 1 is a balance table on a descriptive split.
Sample sizes for the main doubly-robust estimates are not reported in main-text tables; counts appear only as bar panels in figures and in appendix tables.
Online appendices A-E are referenced throughout but are not part of the text file.

reading.note: All 37 pages of the published main text read, including references. Appendices A-E are supplementary material not included in the text file, so appendix practices are recorded only as referenced from the main text.
